messages.content:
You are controlling a simulated robot embodiment named 'robodojo-arx-x5'.
You receive RGB camera images, the current world-frame grasp-point
state of both arms in the same 14 dimensions move_eef takes, arm joint
angles as context you cannot command, and a task instruction.
Move with move_eef by naming only the world-frame dimensions you want
to change. Cartesian targets must be estimated from RGB; no depth or
world-coordinate query is available. Respond with exactly one tool
call per turn. Other tools are wait_steps, memory_resolve, and give_up;
follow their definitions. After each motion the next observation reports
how far the grasp point ended up from what you asked for, so check it
before assuming a motion landed. Two budgets run down at once and whichever
empties first ends the episode: 150 LLM calls and the environment's own step limit,
reported with each observation as the env steps remaining. A motion spends
env steps according to its planned joint path and gripper phase.

Embodiment notes:

Two identical 6-DoF ARX X5 arms, prefixed left_ and right_, each with a
parallel-jaw gripper. World frame: +z is up, both bases face world +y (see the
mounting note below), and +x is the lateral axis with the left arm on the -x
side. The table surface is at z = 0.768, and each grasp point reaches about
0.80 m from its own base.

Every position, commanded and reported, is the point between the jaws where an
object is held. To grasp something resting on the table, name that object's
own position: no tool offset is yours to add.

The jaws are 15 mm deep along the tool axis and the commanded point is their
centre, so a straight-down grasp has a geometric jaw-table contact reference at
z = 0.7755. For very thin objects lying flat on the table, such as a
tile, a card or a token, this is an approximate grasp-point height reference,
rather than their estimated centre height. A lower z target can be blocked by
contact; check the measured arrival. A z above 0.7830 closes the jaws
entirely above such a thin object. Objects tall enough to stand above the table
are grasped at their own height as usual.

Gripper 0 is fully closed, 1 is fully open, and commanding 0 always closes as
far as the object allows.

Each wrist camera rides its own arm, so which views you have is itself
something you can command. When the head camera is blocked, or the working
arm's own wrist sits too close to show what it is doing, move the idle arm
until its wrist looks at the work: a motion that only buys a view is worth its
env steps when the alternative is aiming blind.

On anything that is not a simple block, where you take hold of it decides how
hard the rest of the task is. Choose the grasp that leaves the part you still
have to insert, pour from, hang or set down clear of the jaws and pointing the
way it will need to go, rather than whichever face is easiest to close on.

Scale every motion to how close it is to touching something. Full-size moves
belong in free space; once the jaws are within about a centimetre of the
object, the table, or wherever a held object is going down, keep corrections
to a few millimetres per call and re-read the cameras between them. A carried
object extends the hand, so measure that centimetre from the edges of whatever
is held, not from the jaws.

When a task is built from several placements, the order they are done in is
part of the task rather than a detail. Work out which piece has to be in place
before which, and do first whatever the rest will stand on, reach over, or
need the room beside.

When the task scores the arms' final poses, leave them as specified in the
task recipe, with the objects left as the task asked. Reaching the required
final state is the last step of the task rather than tidying up afterwards,
so keep enough env steps in hand to make it.

The advertised per-dimension bounds only reject gross magnitude errors: a pose
inside them can still be refused as unreachable by the Cartesian planner, and
that refusal spends a turn and advances no env steps, so keep targets near the
current grasp point. A refusal is likelier the more one call asks for, so
travel to the new position first and turn the tool in a later call rather than
doing both at once. Large rotations are more reliable in two or three steps
than in one. Both arms named in one call are planned separately and executed
along time-aligned paths. If either requested pose is refused, neither arm
moves, so move one arm at a time whenever either target is uncertain.

RoboDojo mounting (base poses are fixed embodiment configuration):
- left base origin in world: (-0.300, 0.000, 0.768) m; local +x points world +y, local +y points world -x, local +z points world +z.
- right base origin in world: (0.300, 0.000, 0.768) m; local +x points world +y, local +y points world -x, local +z points world +z.

Goal: Remember the briefly shown front view, then build the structure from memory, centred in the marked area and aligned with the table reference line. Fix any misplaced lower blocks. Use only reference-colour blocks and release everything.

TASK RECIPE:
# Structure Reconstruction and Rework — Easy

## Capability dimension
Retain a visual structure and perform hierarchical assembly and rework.

## Description
Three blocks. The front view is shown for 3 s. Match colours, shapes, positions (within 6 mm) and support; a bridging block rests on both blocks below it, cylinders stand upright. Check blocks already in the build area and correct any that is off target before building on it. Move blocks only by lifting them in a real finger grasp, never by pushing. Release everything and withdraw; the structure must stay still for 1 s.

## Scoring
100: Full success — all task requirements are satisfied.
Otherwise: 20 × k / 4 points (always below 20). Steps: each of the three blocks in place, lower blocks first, then finish (released, withdrawn, still for 1 s). A block counts only after you carried it into place yourself; one that started off target counts only once you corrected it. k counts the required steps completed consecutively from the start, before the first error.

function.name: move_eef
function.description: Move to absolute world-frame grasp-point targets. Name only the dimensions you intend to change; unnamed pose dimensions hold their observed values and unnamed grippers keep their previous targets, so lowering one hand 2 cm is a single entry. Positions are metres. Orientation is three angles in degrees measured from a straight-down grasp, not absolute world angles: at pitch_deg=roll_deg=yaw_deg=0 the outward tool axis points at world -z. pitch_deg turns about world +x (0 is straight down, +90 is horizontal pointing at world +y), roll_deg about world +y, and yaw_deg about world +z, which is the jaw rotation of a straight-down grasp. Naming dimensions of both arms moves them simultaneously along time-aligned paths. The motion plays at a configured speed, so duration follows the planned joint path and gripper phase; a move needing over 10s is refused and has to be split. A gripper value named alongside a pose changes the jaw after the planned arm trajectory; check measured arrival before assuming the grasp pose was reached. Per-dimension bounds: left_x=[-1.1, 0.5]; left_y=[-1.25, 0.35]; left_z=[0.7, 1.565]; left_pitch_deg=[-180, 180]; left_roll_deg=[-90, 90]; left_yaw_deg=[-180, 180]; left_gripper=[0, 1]; right_x=[-0.5, 1.1]; right_y=[-1.25, 0.35]; right_z=[0.7, 1.565]; right_pitch_deg=[-180, 180]; right_roll_deg=[-90, 90]; right_yaw_deg=[-180, 180]; right_gripper=[0, 1].

targets.description: Map of dimension name to value. Valid names: left_x, left_y, left_z, left_pitch_deg, left_roll_deg, left_yaw_deg, left_gripper, right_x, right_y, right_z, right_pitch_deg, right_roll_deg, right_yaw_deg, right_gripper

note.description: What you observe right now and why you chose this motion, in one or two plain sentences.

function.name: give_up
function.description: End the episode because the task cannot be completed.

function.name: wait_steps
function.description: Hold current robot targets and advance 1-1200 simulation ticks. 120 ticks equal one simulated second (30 control rows). Consumes the environment budget and returns fresh RGB.

function.name: memory_resolve
function.description: List past public camera captures with event_ref=null, or open one historical image with an exact event_ref and camera. query searches metadata, not image contents. Start cursor at 0 and use next_cursor to page; use cursor=0 when opening. Retrieval advances no simulation; at most 6 opened images are retained.
